extracted.intended_audience: young aspiring authors, literary men and journalists (early-career)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and moral guidance for young writers and journalists on how to conduct a literary life: whether to make authorship a trade, how to combine it with a profession, how to research and argue in journalism, and how to read and judge other writers. Grounded in Coleridge's experience and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never pursue literature as a trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Never pursue literature as a trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues that with the exception of one extraordinary man, authors without some regular employment are rarely healthy or happy. The necessity of earning money or immediate reputation perverts motives and stuns genius; motives by excess reverse their nature. Literature should not constitute the whole profession or identity of a man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a regular profession or employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Have some regular employment which does not depend on the will of the moment and can be carried on mechanically so that an average quantum of health, spirits, and intellectual exertion suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: manufactory, counting house, law-court, medical practice, the Church. Such a profession provides three hours of leisure unannoyed by alien anxiety and supplies the necessities of life, giving freedom for genial literary work and better domestic happiness and social sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devote talents to competence and genius to tranquil choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Devote your talents to acquiring competence in some known trade or profession, and your genius to objects of tranquil and unbiassed choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division allows talents to secure competence and livelihood while preserving genius for freer, more genuine literary creation, both ennobled by sincere duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit literary labour to leisure hours (quality over quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three hours of leisure, unannoyed by any alien anxiety, will suffice to realize in literature a larger product of what is truly genial than weeks of compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge stresses that leisure writing—looked forward to as recreation—yields better work than forced, continuous literary labour. Avoid turning writing into an urgent economic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid money and immediate reputation as primary motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Money and immediate reputation form only arbitrary and accidental ends of literary labour; the hope of increasing them often stimulates but the necessity of acquiring them will convert stimulant into narcotic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When financial necessity becomes the motive, it usually diminishes the quality of genius-driven work. Keep motives salutary and intrinsic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do strict self-examination before choosing authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrutinize whether indolence, restlessness, or vanity impatient for immediate gratification have tampered with judgment and assumed the vizard of humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogue scruples, reduce them to distinct form, ensure you have read fundamental works on the subject, and seek counsel from elder contemporaries who faced similar scruples and can testify to the consequences of rash decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay rash decisions until manhood and temperance develop
rubrics_metrics.description: Time spent in delay is time won: manhood advances, knowledge increases, judgment strengthens, and temperance of feelings grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A postponement of an irrevocable step allows maturity and prevents decisions later regretted. Even if no change results, delay avoids the inward censure of rashness and vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let literature constitute your entire identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be not merely a man of letters; let literature augment your arms but not constitute the coat or fill the escutcheon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monomania—having other social roles prevents being perceived solely as an author, aids conversation, and protects domestic and social happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider professions compatible with literary pursuits (e.g., the Church)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church (and other established professions) presents a profession in which one may unite wide literary schemes with strict professional duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge details advantages: access to parish life, connection with families, encouragement of learning, and a decorum favourable to genius. He argues the established Church is an effective, unburdensome patronage of learning in a Protestant country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid becoming a mere servant of the press (over-publishing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the habit of sending every passing thought to the press; excessive or premature authorship makes one a mere servant of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Herder: authorship used too early or immoderately makes the head wild and the heart empty; those who publish every thought risk becoming 'a book-setter'—a mechanical transmitter of trivialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the best and most fundamental works before deciding or publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be certain that you have read with a docile mind and favourable disposition the best and most fundamental works on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-grounded knowledge base helps prevent rash or uninformed departures from received opinion and supports conscientious decision-making about a literary career.

rubrics_metrics.name: In journalism, conduct on fixed and announced principles
rubrics_metrics.description: If undertaking editorial/journalistic work, conduct the paper on certain fixed and announced principles and do not deviate from them in favour of any party or event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge required this condition when accepting the Morning Post editorship: consistent, declared principles secure credibility and avoid partisan compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define impartiality as adherence to announced principles, not abuse or pandering
rubrics_metrics.description: Impartiality means an honest and enlightened adherence to a code of intelligible principles previously announced; not indiscriminate abuse, not indulgence of an editor’s malignant passions, and not flattering the envy and cupidity of the mob.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being moderately anti-ministerial but principled can be more useful and credible than slavish eulogy or pandering to popular vices; genuine impartiality attracts readership without ministerial patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place events and questions in a moral point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the questions and events of the day in a moral point of view; give dignity to measures by tracing their policy or impolicy to permanent principles, and give interest to principles by applying them to individual measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge claims this practice enriches political essays and helps readers see the connection between principle and practice; it contributed to the Morning Post's influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical analogy and primary contemporary sources in political analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: On every great occurrence endeavour to discover in past history the event that most nearly resembled it; procure contemporary historians, memorialists, and pamphleteers; subtract points of difference from likeness and judge accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge describes composing comparative essays (e.g., France under Napoleon vs Rome under the Caesars) using original documents and contemporaries' accounts to ground judgments and to predict outcomes with philosophical tact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek original documents and have a philosophic tact for important facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Arm yourself with the original documents of the past and authentic accounts of the present; have a philosophic tact for what is truly important in facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer facts and details excluded from modern compilers; such original-source grounded judgment reduces error in forecasting national events and strengthens political argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable and explanatory reading of visionary or fanatic writers
rubrics_metrics.description: In reading works of religious fanatics or visionaries, resolve to explain strange incidents by application of received and ascertained laws rather than suspecting intentional falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until you understand a writer’s ignorance, presume yourself ignorant of his understanding: track the causes affecting the mind (physiological, psychological) and follow traces without imputing deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain seriousness and avoid triviality; genuine labour is visible in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing should not be mere triviality; good prose requires labour and serious thought rather than mere rhetorical frippery, excessive refinement, or paradox-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge defends his own prose against charges of obscurity and paradox by asserting his works show the toil of thought; writers should aim for substance and avoid 'tricking out' others' thoughts or mere verbal ornament.
